::: {.fi-standfirst}
Most health tools hand you an answer and hide the argument behind it. **FRESH**
starts at the argument.
:::

## The problem worth working on

Ask whether a food is healthy and you can get five credible answers from five
expert systems, all published, all defensible. The consensus holds at the level of
slogans, eat more vegetables and less added sugar, and it collapses food by food,
which is exactly the level that labels, front-of-pack claims, school and hospital
procurement, and reformulation targets all run on. "We know what's healthy" is true
as a slogan and false as an instruction.

So the question is not how to pick a winner. It is what to do when the credible
sources disagree, and how to hand someone a usable answer without lying about how
sure it is.

## The statistics are the spine

A number without its uncertainty is not an answer. That commitment shows up in
unglamorous places: quality is never collapsed to a single score, contradictions
between studies have to be explained before they are declared, measurement error is
carried from the raw input through to the value on screen, and every extracted
figure keeps a trail back to its source. Nothing counts as settled here until it
reproduces a published benchmark, standard error included.

Disagreement gets measured rather than smoothed away. When five systems rate the
same food, the spread is the finding, and foods where the systems cannot agree are
labeled as contested rather than quietly assigned a number.

## Belief is data too

What people believe is not error to be corrected on the way to the real analysis.
Beliefs steer which questions get funded, which products get made, and who ends up
better off for the science. So beliefs get measured with the same seriousness as
composition and effect sizes, then compared against the expert record.

The gaps come back specific. Some foods the public judges harshly that the evidence
treats kindly, some it lets off easy, and some the experts cannot agree on either,
which makes public confusion an entirely reasonable response. Those three cases call
for different work, and naming which is which is an education agenda, food by food,
rather than a scolding.

## Food first, then the rest of a life

Food comes first because it is the hardest case: expert systems clash most openly
there, measurement is noisiest, and public belief has drifted furthest from the
evidence. The methods are not about food. The same machinery reaches sleep,
movement, mind and mood, social connection and loneliness, self-care, substance use,
biological age, health literacy, and the place you live, read from what you report,
what you wear, and what your blood says, scored per domain with the uncertainty
kept visible.

## Where the effort goes instead

Health effort goes to widening access, to definition fights that burn political
capital over what counts as ultraprocessed, to narrow policies that work as
bandages, to pointing at personal behavior. Those matter. But the information
itself gets treated as solved, and it is not solved.

Better information cures nothing on its own. It is the cheapest lever almost nobody
is pulling, and it feeds the others: clearer definitions make better labels and
better procurement, and honest, uncertainty-aware information leaves less room for
the misinformation that fills a vacuum.

## What it is made of

Five engines sit behind the tools and essays here. None of them is really about
food.

| Engine | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Evidence** | Reads the published literature end to end: finds the studies, checks trial quality and trustworthiness, re-pools the effects, and keeps a trail from every claim back to its source. |
| **Consensus** | Reconciles competing expert rating systems into a consensus with the disagreement measured and reported, never hidden inside an average. |
| **Risk** | Combines risk models with trial-derived effects to estimate what a change is worth for particular people and places, with uncertainty propagated rather than dropped. |
| **Decision** | Turns contradictory signals into one personal answer that shows its own doubt. |
| **Well-being** | Scores well-being across an open set of life domains from self-report, wearable, and biomarker inputs, per domain and combined. |

## Who this is for

Anyone who wants to see the evidence for themselves: people making decisions about
their own health, researchers who want the provenance, and the people writing the
labels, the guidance, and the policy. The essays are the argument in public. The
tools let you check it.
